title: Kiki Katese's Case for an Ice-Cream Shop in Butare
dek: A Rwandan playwright persuaded two Brooklyn ice-cream makers that her women drummers should sell something few Rwandans had ever tasted.

story.event: Proposing and opening an ice-cream shop run by the women of the Ingoma Nshya drumming troupe
story.summary: After meeting Jennie Dundas of Brooklyn's Blue Marble ice-cream shop at a Sundance Institute theatre workshop, the Rwandan playwright Odile Gakire (Kiki) Katese proposed that women from Ingoma Nshya, the drumming troupe she founded, open an ice-cream shop. With seed money raised by the nonprofit Blue Marble Dreams and a donated soft-serve machine, the drummers' cooperative opened Inzozi Nziza (Sweet Dreams) in Butare in mid-2010. It was nearly breaking even by 2011 and, by 2014, no longer relied on early support from the Japan International Cooperation Agency.
paragraphs: At a Sundance Institute theatre workshop in the late 2000s, the American actor Jennie Dundas shared ice cream she had flown in from Blue Marble, the Brooklyn shop she co-owned. One of those who tasted it was Odile Gakire Katese, known as Kiki, a Rwandan playwright and drummer. By one account she took Dundas aside and said, "I want to talk to you about ice cream."

Katese lived in Butare, the university town in southern Rwanda, where she had founded Ingoma Nshya, the country's first women's drumming troupe, in a tradition that kept the drum for men. Its members came from both sides of the 1994 genocide: survivors and widows, and wives of men imprisoned for the killings. The group had grown from about 25 women to about 100 and was looking for work that could include them. Ice cream was almost unknown in Rwanda, and most of the women had never tasted it.

Dundas's partner, Alexis Miesen, was doubtful at first. "Hospitals and schools seemed more in order," she said later. She remembered Katese's answer: "There's no room to dream when survival is the only goal." Katese told filmmakers that people needed a space to renew themselves, "especially in Rwanda where people are broken." After an exploratory visit, the Brooklyn partners formed a nonprofit, Blue Marble Dreams, to raise seed money. The drummers formed a cooperative and chose committee leaders by lining up openly behind candidates, insisting that every count be read aloud. Because Rwandan cows give little cream and power cuts were common, they settled on soft-serve from a donated machine.

Inzozi Nziza, Kinyarwanda for Sweet Dreams, opened on Butare's main street in mid-2010. Not every first taste went well. Chantal Kabatesi, who first tried ice cream at 35, told NPR it was "like eating hailstones", and one customer, Miesen recalled, asked whether it had to be so cold. There was a deeper obstacle too: eating in the street is thought shameful in Rwanda, so carts and stands were out.

By 2011 Miesen said the shop was nearly breaking even most months, though trade fell when the university was on holiday. By 2014 it no longer depended on early support from the Japan International Cooperation Agency, and Katese was talking about opening shops in other towns.

quote.text: Love thine own soul, and comfort thy heart: and remove sorrow far from thee; for sorrow hath destroyed many, and there is no profit therein.
quote.translator: Revised Version of the Apocrypha (1895), as selected in the Wisdom of the East series (1910)
quote.source_title: The Wisdom of the Apocrypha, Project Gutenberg eBook #77250
quote.connection: Ben Sira, a teacher in Jerusalem, treats comforting your own heart as a way of loving your own soul, not as an indulgence to be earned. Katese made a similar case for something sweet in a country still grieving, while insisting that learning to cry again belonged to recovery as well.

reflection: Miesen's first doubt was a reasonable one, and you may hear it in yourself: with so much that is urgent, anything pleasant can look like a distraction. Katese did not argue that roads and hospitals mattered less. Her point was that people who are only surviving have no room left to imagine anything else.

That holds for one person as well as for a country. On long days the small things go first: a meal eaten sitting down, a walk, music, an hour with someone you love. Ben Sira does not call these rewards for finishing the work. He calls comforting your own heart a way of looking after your soul.
invitation: Choose one small, sweet thing to have today, ice cream if you like, and sit down somewhere to enjoy it properly instead of eating it on the move.

research_notes: Dates disagree in three places. (1) The Sundance meeting: Edible Brooklyn (2011) says a 2008 Sundance Institute workshop; the filmmakers writing for Al Jazeera (2010) say Katese was invited to the Sundance Institute Theatre Lab in 2009; the Optimist Daily gives no year. The story says 'in the late 2000s'. (2) Ingoma Nshya's founding: The New Times (2019) and a German theatre listing say 2004, and Farm Radio says Chantal Kabatesi joined in 2004; Al Jazeera and the film's Wikipedia article say 2005. The story gives no founding year. (3) The opening: the Optimist Daily says June 2010, Edible Brooklyn summer 2010, and Al Jazeera (31 October 2010) describes the shop as a reality; Farm Radio (2014) says the women launched the business at the end of 2010. The story uses mid-2010 and approx_date 2010-06. Membership: Farm Radio says the group grew from 25 to 100 members; the story says 'about'. Katese's spoken quotation 'I want to talk to you about ice cream' rests on the Optimist Daily alone and is introduced with 'by one account'. 'There's no room to dream when survival is the only goal' is Miesen's recollection of Katese's argument (Edible Brooklyn) and is attributed to that memory. Katese's 'especially in Rwanda where people are broken' was said to the documentary makers and quoted by Edible Brooklyn. Funding is set to 'mixed': seed money came from the nonprofit Blue Marble Dreams, the shop was a cooperative business (the Optimist Daily calls it a for-profit cooperative in a joint venture with Blue Marble Dreams), and Farm Radio reports early support from JICA. Financial outcome: Miesen's 2011 'nearly breaking even in most months' and Farm Radio's 2014 'now self-sufficient' are reported as such; the Optimist Daily's 2012 figures (about 50 cones a day, a small serving priced like a soda) are not used. The town is Butare, in Huye District (renamed Huye in 2006); the story uses Butare as the sources do. The Ben Sira edition has no verse numbers; the passage is Ecclesiasticus 30:23 in the usual numbering, in the Revised Version wording the 1910 selection follows ('sorrow hath destroyed many'). The NYT review of the film (Miriam Bale, 31 October 2013) and The EastAfrican's profile were blocked to automated requests and are not cited.
